modelAnswer: Vaccination is an effective method of preventing infectious diseases by stimulating the body's specific immune system to produce antibodies and immunological memory against particular pathogens without causing the disease itself. When a vaccine containing weakened or inactivated antigens is administered, B lymphocytes recognize these antigens and produce specific antibodies, while T cells develop memory. Upon exposure to the actual pathogen, the immune system rapidly produces antibodies and activates memory cells, providing immediate protection and preventing infection or reducing disease severity. This artificial active immunity offers long-lasting protection and has successfully controlled many infectious diseases globally.
